extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, IP practitioners, and policymakers focused on Indian patent law
extracted.subtask_short: Indian patent revocation and public interest
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on grounds for revocation, compulsory licensing, government use, and public-interest limitations under the Indian Patents Act (including statutory tests like novelty, inventive step, sufficiency, secrecy, source disclosure, and working in India).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness / Inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: That the invention so far as claimed in any claim is obvious or does not involve any inventive step having regard to what was publicly known or publicly used in India or what was published in India or elsewhere before the priority date of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness means something 'easily perceived by the senses or grasped by the mind' or 'clearly or plainly evident' to a person having fair knowledge of the subject. The manner in which the invention was arrived at is relevant. The assessment is with reference to the 'state of art' and whether a skilled person could carry out the development without any substantial inventive step. If subject matter appears obvious it does not involve an inventive step and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention is not useful (lack of utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground for revocation when a patent has been obtained for an invention which is not useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Not useful' means the invention will not work (either it may not operate at all or may not provide the desired result as mentioned in the specification). Utility is judged with reference to the state of the art at the date of the patent. Practical or commercial usefulness is not required for sufficiency of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification not sufficiently and fairly describing the invention (sufficiency of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification must describe an embodiment of the invention claimed in each of the claims and the description must be sufficient to enable those in the industry concerned to put it into effect without their making further invention; the description must be fair and not unnecessarily difficult to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instructions for working the invention must be sufficient for a person in India possessing average skill and knowledge of the art to work the invention. The specification should disclose the best method known to the applicant for performing the invention if entitled to claim protection for it. Sufficiency is judged on the merits of the specification; no hard and fast rule can be laid down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim not clearly defined and not fairly based
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) The scope of any claim of the complete specification is not sufficiently and clearly defined; and/or (ii) any claim of the complete specification is not fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Fairly based’ means the patentee should get a monopoly exactly sufficient to protect his invention as disclosed, but must not claim more monopoly than is justified by the disclosure. A patent is granted in lieu of disclosure to the public, so claims must be commensurate with the disclosed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent obtained by false suggestion or representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be revoked on the ground that it was obtained on false suggestion or representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False suggestion or representation may relate to the specification or any fact or statement required to be made in connection with the grant. There is no limitation on the nature of such falsehood; intent/knowledge that it is false is relevant in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject of claims not a patentable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of any claim of the complete specification is not an invention within the meaning of the Act or is otherwise not patentable under the Act (e.g., exclusions under sections 3 and 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ground captures statutory exclusions and other legal doctrines rendering claimed subject-matter outside patentable subject matter under Indian law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention secretly used before the priority date (secret prior use)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification was secretly used in India, otherwise than as excepted, before the priority date of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior secret use will invalidate the patent except for certain conditions (see section 64(3)). Secret use done for trial or experimental purposes as specified may be excepted. No account is to be taken of personal documents or secret trial or secret use for some clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose information regarding foreign application (section 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant for the patent has failed to disclose to the Controller the information required by section 8 or has furnished information which in any material particular was false to his knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant conceals matters or supplies information that is known by him to be false, the patent may be revoked. If information was furnished believing it to be true but it turned out false in fact, the revocation ground may not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compliance of secrecy direction (section 35)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant has contravened any secrecy direction issued by the Controller under section 35, the patent granted shall be revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 35 permits directions prohibiting or restricting publication/communication of information relevant to defence; contravention of such directions is a ground of revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave to amend specification obtained by fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: If permission to amend the application or complete specification was obtained by fraud, that is a ground of opposition/revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Controller and High Court have powers to allow amendments, but amendments obtained by fraudulent means can invalidate the patent or be set aside in revocation proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification wrongly mentioning or not disclosing geographical origin of biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be revoked if the applicant had wrongly mentioned or did not disclose the source or geographical origin of biological material used for the invention in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision addresses benefit-sharing and disclosure obligations for biological material, including considerations regarding indigenous communities and permissions that may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention anticipated by traditional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be revoked if any detail claimed in the specification is anticipated by knowledge available orally or otherwise within any local or indigenous community in India or anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional knowledge (oral or otherwise) that predates the priority date can be treated as anticipation and defeat patentability; this is explicitly recognized as a ground of revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to anticipation and secret use
rubrics_metrics.description: No account shall be taken of personal documents or secret trial or secret use for certain anticipation and prior-use provisions; importation into India of a product made abroad by a claimed process may constitute knowledge/use in India of the invention on date of importation, except where importation has been for reasonable trial or experiment only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute carves out exceptions where secret trials/uses and limited importations do not count as public knowledge or use; these exceptions must be considered particularly when applying clauses on novelty and obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and public-interest principles of the patent system (section 83)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted to encourage inventions and to secure that the inventions are worked in India on a commercial scale and to the fullest extent reasonably practicable without undue delay; not granted merely to enable patentees to enjoy a monopoly for importation; protection should promote technological innovation, transfer and dissemination of technology to mutual advantage; patents should not impede public health and nutrition and should promote public interest; patents should be available at reasonably affordable prices; patent rights should not be abused to unreasonably restrain trade or adversely affect international transfer of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles guide interpretation of working, compulsory licensing, revocation in public interest, and other remedial provisions: emphasis on working in India, technology transfer and public health concerns, and prevention of abuse of patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licence: primary statutory grounds (section 84)
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time after the expiration of three years from the date of grant of the patent, any person interested may apply for a compulsory licence if (a) the reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied; or (b) the patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price; or (c) the patented invention is not worked in the territory of India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application must contain the applicant’s interest and particulars/facts on which it is based. Controller may grant a licence on terms he deems fit if satisfied that one or more grounds exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controller's considerations when deciding a compulsory licence
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering an application for compulsory licence the Controller shall take into account: the nature of the invention; the time elapsed since grant and measures already taken by patentees or licensees to make full use of the invention; the ability of the applicant to work the invention to the public advantage; the capacity of the applicant to undertake the risk in providing capital and working the invention; whether the applicant has made efforts to obtain a licence from the patentee on reasonable terms and such efforts have not been successful within a reasonable period (normally not exceeding 6 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors guide the discretionary balancing of interests. The 'reasonable period' for negotiation is generally construed as not exceeding 6 months. The clause about prior efforts is not applicable in cases of national emergency, extreme urgency, public non-commercial use, or established anticompetitive practices by the patentee. The Controller shall not be required to take into account matters subsequent to the making of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and tests for 'reasonable requirements of the public'
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of compulsory licensing, the reasonable requirements of the public shall be deemed not to have been satisfied if, by reason of the patentee's refusal to grant licences on reasonable terms: (i) an existing trade or industry or its development or establishment of new trade/industry in India is prejudiced; or (ii) the demand for the patented article has not been met to an adequate extent or on reasonable terms; or (iii) a market for export of the patented article manufactured in India is not being supplied or developed; or (iv) the establishment or development of commercial activities in India is prejudiced; or if by reason of conditions imposed by the patentee on grants of licences or purchase/use, manufacture/use/sale of materials not protected by the patent or establishment/development of trade is prejudiced; or if the patentee imposes exclusive grant-back, prevents challenges to validity, or engages in coercive package licensing; or if the patented invention is not being worked in India on a commercial scale to an adequate extent or to the fullest extent reasonably practicable; or if working is prevented or hindered by importation from abroad by the patentee or persons claiming under him or by persons purchasing from him, or other persons against whom the patentee is not taking proceedings for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a broad multi-factor test indicating circumstances where public requirements are unmet and justifying compulsory licensing or other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special provisions for compulsory licence on central government notification (section 92)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory licence can be granted at any time after grant of the patent in circumstances of national emergency, extreme urgency or public non-commercial use (including public health crises). The Central Government may notify that compulsory licences should be granted, and the Controller shall on application grant a licence on terms he thinks fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid delay, general procedure and opposition provisions may be waived in such circumstances. In settling terms the Controller shall endeavour to secure that articles manufactured under the patent are available to the public at the lowest prices consistent with patentees deriving a reasonable advantage from their rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licence for manufacture and export of pharmaceuticals (section 92A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory licence is available for manufacture and export of patented pharmaceutical products to any country having insufficient or no manufacturing capacity in the pharmaceutical sector for the concerned product to address public health problems, provided compulsory licence has been granted by such country or such country has allowed importation from India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent office may not insist on compulsory licence having been granted by the importing country in every case; other arrangements (e.g., general license or lack of patent protection in the importing country) may suffice. Proceedings may be published when such an application is filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation of patents: statutory list (section 64)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to the Act, a patent may be revoked by Appellate Board/High Court on petition of any person interested or Central Government on grounds enumerated in section 64 clauses (a)–(q) (e.g., earlier valid claim, wrong applicant, not an invention, not novel, obvious, not useful, insufficiency, unclear scope or not fairly based, false suggestion, not patentable, secret prior use, failure to disclose foreign application info, contravention of secrecy directions/section 39, amendment obtained by fraud, wrong source/geographical origin disclosure for biological material, anticipated by local/indigenous knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 64 consolidates the statutory grounds for revocation; many of these are expanded elsewhere in the chapter (novelty, inventive step, sufficiency, disclosure obligations, secrecy, fraud, traditional knowledge). Procedural aspects (who may petition, notices) are also prescribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation in public interest (section 66)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Central Government is of opinion that a patent or the mode in which it is exercised is mischievous to the State or generally prejudicial to the public, it may, after giving the patentee an opportunity to be heard and declaring so in the Official Gazette, cause the patent to be deemed revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a discretionary power to address misuse or public prejudice beyond the individual statutory grounds in section 64; an opportunity to be heard is required before declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation for non-working (section 85)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a compulsory licence has been granted, the Central Government or any person interested may, after the expiration of two years from the date of the order granting the first compulsory licence, apply to the Controller for an order revoking the patent on the ground that the patented invention has not been worked in India or reasonable requirements of the public have not been satisfied or the patented invention is not available at a reasonably affordable price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a targeted remedy to revoke patents that remain unworked or that fail public-interest working obligations even after compulsory licences have been tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use of inventions (section 100)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding anything in the Act, at any time after an application for a patent has been filed or a patent granted, the Central Government and any person authorised by it may use the invention for the purposes of Government in accordance with the Chapter's provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention had been recorded, tested or tried by or on behalf of the Government before the priority date (other than due to disclosure by the patentee), such use may be free of royalty or remuneration. Otherwise use is to be on agreed terms or terms determined by the High Court; the patentee must be notified (except in emergencies/non-commercial use) and paid not more than adequate remuneration considering the economic value of the use. Uses may include making, using, exercising, vending or importing covered articles for government purposes and can include sale on a non-commercial basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition of inventions/patents by Central Government (section 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Central Government may, if satisfied that it is necessary that an invention (application or patent) should be acquired for a public purpose, publish a notification and the invention/patent and all rights shall stand transferred to and vested in the Central Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice is to be given to the applicant/patentee and persons of record. The Government shall pay compensation agreed or, failing agreement, determined by the High Court taking into account expenditure incurred, term of patent, period and manner of working, profits made by patentee or licensee, and other relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant of patents subject to conditions (section 47) — government/research exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant of a patent is subject to conditions that: (1) any machine, apparatus or article or article made by a patented process may be made or imported by or on behalf of the Government for its own use; (2) any patented process may be used by or on behalf of the Government for its own use; (3) any patented article or process may be used by any person for the purpose merely of experiment or research including imparting instructions to pupils; and (4) in case of a patented medicine or drug, the medicine may be imported by the Government for its own use or for distribution in specified government-maintained institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standing limitations on patent rights to allow government use, research/experimental use and specified public-health distribution by the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government interference where drug cost prohibitively high
rubrics_metrics.description: Government can interfere if the cost of a medicine is prohibitively high, under the public-interest and working/compulsory licensing provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High cost of medicines is an explicit policy concern underlying compulsory licence and government-use provisions; affordability is a basis for remedial action including compulsory licence, government use, acquisition or revocation in public interest.
